extracted.intended_audience: recipients of Federal financial assistance (schools, colleges, universities), Title IX coordinators, school administrators, policymakers, and stakeholders commenting on Title IX rulemaking
extracted.subtask_description: Clarifying and implementing the Department of Education's three‑pronged regulatory definition of 'sexual harassment' under §106.30 for education programs and activities, including how each prong applies and how recipients must respond.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three‑pronged definition of sexual harassment (§106.30)
rubrics_metrics.description: Sexual harassment means conduct on the basis of sex that satisfies one or more of the following: (1) quid pro quo harassment by any recipient employee; (2) unwelcome conduct on the basis of sex that is so severe, pervasive, and objectively offensive that it effectively denies a person equal access to education (the Davis formulation); and (3) sexual assault (with reference to Clery Act/VAWA offenses).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This three‑part definition adopts the Supreme Court's formulation while adapting it for administrative enforcement under Title IX. It is intended to capture categories of misconduct likely to impede educational access while avoiding a chill on free speech and academic freedom. The definition is broad in scope overall and is the baseline for when a recipient must respond under Title IX, while recipients retain discretion to address other misconduct outside this definition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prong (1) — Quid pro quo harassment is per se actionable
rubrics_metrics.description: Quid pro quo harassment by any recipient employee (conditioning an educational benefit on sexual cooperation) is actionable under §106.30.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department treats quid pro quo harassment as per se actionable—that is, it does not require inquiry into severity, pervasiveness, or objective offensiveness. The rule clarifies that the 'bargain' may be communicated expressly or impliedly. 'Consenting' to unwelcome sexual conduct or avoiding adverse consequences does not negate that quid pro quo occurred. The prong is framed as applying to recipient employees; commenters asked about expanding to non‑employees (e.g., student leaders, volunteers), but the regulatory text applies to employees.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prong (2) — Davis standard (severe, pervasive, objectively offensive)
rubrics_metrics.description: Unwelcome conduct on the basis of sex that is so severe, pervasive, and objectively offensive that it effectively denies a person equal access to education (the Davis formulation) constitutes sexual harassment under §106.30.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The elements of severity, pervasiveness, objective offensiveness, and denial of equal access are to be determined by a reasonable person standard (a 'reasonable person in the shoes of the complainant'). This narrow, tailored standard is intended to avoid First Amendment problems by prohibiting speech/expression only when seriousness and impact outweigh free‑speech concerns. Age, abilities, and relative positions of authority should be considered in the reasonable person analysis. The Department emphasizes these elements focus on the nature of the misconduct, not the victim's individualized reaction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prong (3) — Sexual assault and Clery Act/VAWA offenses are per se actionable
rubrics_metrics.description: Sexual assault (and the three additional Clery Act/VAWA offenses: dating violence, domestic violence, and stalking) are included in the third prong of §106.30 and treated as per se sexual harassment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unlike the Davis formulation, these offenses do not require proof of severity, pervasiveness, or objective offensiveness— the Department assumes victims of quid pro quo or these Clery/VAWA offenses have been effectively denied equal access to education. The final regulations reference Clery Act and VAWA statutes (rather than Clery regulations) and broadly incorporate the Clery Act definition of sexual assault as used by the FBI UCR.

rubrics_metrics.name: "On the basis of sex" is required for all prongs
rubrics_metrics.description: The phrase 'on the basis of sex' has been moved from the second prong into the introductory sentence so that any conduct meeting any prong must be 'on the basis of sex.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whether conduct is 'on the basis of sex' does not require probing the respondent's subjective motive. Conduct that is sexual in nature, or references or is aimed at a particular sex, suffices. The Department follows Supreme Court approaches (Gebser, Davis) in interpreting this element without requiring proof of subjective intent or statistical disparate impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable person perspective for evaluating Davis elements
rubrics_metrics.description: The Davis elements (severe, pervasive, objectively offensive, and effective denial of equal access) are to be evaluated under a reasonable person standard.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluators should adopt the perspective of a reasonable person 'in the shoes of the complainant' and take into account ages, abilities, and relative positions of authority. This clarification is intended to ensure complainants' individualized reactions are not the determinative focus and to provide clearer expectations for recipients when identifying and responding to Title IX sexual harassment incidents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Speech/expression distinction and First Amendment considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: The regulations are designed to further Title IX's non‑discrimination mandate while acknowledging the unique importance of First Amendment freedoms in education; verbal/expression‑based harassment is subject to a narrowly tailored standard to avoid chilling protected speech.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Davis 'catch‑all' that covers purely verbal harassment requires severity/pervasiveness/objective offensiveness to avoid prior restraints on speech and academic freedom. Physical conduct and crimes (quid pro quo; Clery/VAWA offenses) raise fewer constitutional concerns and are treated as per se actionable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recipients must respond to quid pro quo and Clery/VAWA offenses without inquiry into severity/pervasiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: When incidents of quid pro quo harassment or Clery Act/VAWA offenses are reported to the recipient, the recipient must respond without inquiring into the severity or pervasiveness of such conduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This obligation gives clear direction that certain categories of misconduct automatically trigger a Title IX response. Recipients still retain discretion to address other misconduct that does not meet Title IX's definition through their own policies or under state law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coverage of gender harassment and unwanted sexual attention under the Davis prong
rubrics_metrics.description: Verbal and nonverbal behaviors that derogate, demean, or humiliate an individual based on sex ('gender harassment') and 'unwanted sexual attention' are covered under §106.30 if they meet the Davis elements (severe, pervasive, objectively offensive).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department interprets the second prong's language to encompass what NASEM labels 'gender harassment' where the conduct is sufficiently serious/frequent to meet the reasonable person Davis standard. Thus common but nonsevere gendered insults could be outside Title IX even if harmful, though recipients may address them through other policies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technology‑neutral application (cyber‑harassment included)
rubrics_metrics.description: The definition of sexual harassment does not depend on the method by which the harassment is carried out; use of email, the internet, or other technologies may constitute sexual harassment as much as in‑person conduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commenters urged explicit reference to online/cyber‑harassment; the Department's approach is method‑neutral. Whether cyber‑harassment meets a prong of §106.30 depends on the same substance‑based tests (quid pro quo, Davis elements, Clery/VAWA offenses).

rubrics_metrics.name: Grooming behaviors and other conduct not explicitly enumerated
rubrics_metrics.description: Grooming behaviors (gradual sexualization of relationships, inappropriate jokes, sharing pornographic material, inappropriate access to locker rooms, singling out students) are not identified as a distinct category but may constitute sexual harassment if they meet one or more §106.30 prongs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department acknowledges grooming as a concern; some grooming conduct may fall within §106.30, while other suspect or inappropriate behaviors that do not meet Title IX's definition should nevertheless be recognized and addressed by recipients outside Title IX obligations (e.g., discipline, child‑welfare reporting).

rubrics_metrics.name: Recipients' ability to address conduct outside Title IX
rubrics_metrics.description: Even where conduct does not meet §106.30's definition of sexual harassment, recipients retain authority and discretion to address such misconduct via other policies, state laws, or disciplinary procedures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department does not intend these final regulations to preclude recipients from responding to a wider range of inappropriate or harmful conduct. Title IX compliance does not obviate obligations under other Federal or State laws; differences between definitions under Title IX and state law do not relieve recipients from complying with all applicable laws.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity and openness of the definition to capture evolving misconduct
rubrics_metrics.description: §106.30 aims to be clear enough that victims, perpetrators, and recipients understand what conduct constitutes Title IX sexual harassment while remaining sufficiently open‑ended to capture novel forms of misconduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department likens sexual harassment to 'fraud' as a broad generic term—open‑endedness is intentional to avoid foreclosing behaviors that may be actionable. The regulation balances clarity with flexibility to encompass 'multifarious means' by which sex‑based misconduct can impede educational access.
